annotations.note: The pairing echoes the chapter's opening confession that the horror of whiteness is 'mystical and well nigh ineffable' — muteness is thus not merely a descriptive category but a recurrence of Ishmael's own stated inability to articulate the terror, linking the epistemological problem of the narrator to the phenomenological effect of whiteness itself.

annotations.anchor: unimaginative mind
annotations.note: The distinction between the imaginative and unimaginative mind is the chapter's central epistemological hinge, introduced in the paragraph beginning 'And though, doubtless, some at least of the imaginative impressions about to be presented may have been shared by most men.' The 'unimaginative mind' here is the same figure who cannot follow another 'into these halls' — Melville is closing a bracket opened earlier in the chapter and signaling that the examples to follow are addressed only to readers who have already passed that threshold.

annotations.anchor: prime agent in exaggerating the terror of objects otherwise terrible
annotations.note: The phrase 'otherwise terrible' is crucial and easily overlooked: Melville is not claiming whiteness creates terror from nothing, but that it amplifies pre-existing terror — a more defensible and philosophically precise claim. This modifies the polar bear footnote's argument (that the bear is already ferocious) and anticipates the closing cosmological argument that whiteness is an 'intensifying agent,' not a primary cause. The logical structure of the whole chapter depends on this distinction.

paragraphs.passage: I know that, to the common apprehension, this phenomenon of whiteness is not confessed to be the prime agent in exaggerating the terror of objects otherwise terrible; nor to the unimaginative mind is there aught of terror in those appearances whose awfulness to another mind almost solely consists in this one phenomenon, especially when exhibited under any form at all approaching to muteness or universality. What I mean by these two statements may perhaps be respectively elucidated by the following examples.

annotations.anchor: the lead assures him he is still off soundings
annotations.note: The lead: a weighted line dropped overboard to measure water depth. "Off soundings" means the water is too deep to reach bottom — i.e., no hidden rocks. The instrument rationally confirms safety, yet the dread persists.

annotations.anchor: shoals of combed white bears were swimming round him
annotations.note: Recalls the chapter's earlier invocation of "the white bear of the poles" as a transcendent horror; the simile imports that already-established terror directly into the nautical scene.

annotations.anchor: heart and helm they both go down
annotations.note: Reading: the zeugma yoking an emotional state to a physical ship's instrument enacts the chapter's argument — irrational whiteness-dread overrides both courage and seamanship simultaneously, collapsing the distinction between inner and outer navigation.

annotations.anchor: called from his hammock
annotations.note: The mariner is summoned from sleep — a liminal, vulnerable state — which heightens the irrational quality of the dread. The chapter's argument depends on stripping away rational defenses; catching the sailor between sleep and waking enacts that stripping before the whiteness even appears.

annotations.anchor: milky whiteness
annotations.note: "Milky" recurs pointedly throughout the chapter — "milk-white steeds," "milk-white fog," and later "muffled rollings of a milky sea" in the colt passage that directly echoes this scene. The word choice is not incidental: it links the nautical horror to the chapter's closing synthesis, where the milky sea becomes one of Ishmael's own terror-signs alongside the buffalo robe.

annotations.anchor: starts to vigilance, and feels just enough of trepidation to sharpen all his faculties
annotations.note: Melville carefully distinguishes useful fear — the auditory alarm of breakers producing functional trepidation — from the paralyzing dread of whiteness. This contrast is the structural hinge of the 'First' example: rational fear sharpens; irrational whiteness-dread disables. The annotation on 'heart and helm they both go down' captures the collapse but misses that Melville has already set up the positive counterexample here.

annotations.anchor: encircling headlands
annotations.note: The headlands are the rational explanation the mariner's mind reaches for — a geographic cause for the white water (surf, shoals). Melville embeds the rationalization inside the simile itself, then immediately dissolves it: the 'bears' displace the headlands, and the lead-line dissolves the shoal hypothesis. The sentence performs the very process of rational explanation failing that the paragraph argues for.

annotations.anchor: never rests till blue water is under him again
annotations.note: The relief of 'blue water' directly anticipates — and is answered by — the chapter's closing image of the 'colourless, all-colour' white that underlies all hues. Blue water is safety because it is coloured, particular, bounded; the white sea is terror because it prefigures the 'dumb blankness' of a universe stripped of colour. The mariner's instinct here is the embodied version of the chapter's final philosophical argument.

paragraphs.passage: First: The mariner, when drawing nigh the coasts of foreign lands, if by night he hear the roar of breakers, starts to vigilance, and feels just enough of trepidation to sharpen all his faculties; but under precisely similar circumstances, let him be called from his hammock to view his ship sailing through a midnight sea of milky whiteness—as if from encircling headlands shoals of combed white bears were swimming round him, then he feels a silent, superstitious dread; the shrouded phantom of the whitened waters is horrible to him as a real ghost; in vain the lead assures him he is still off soundings; heart and helm they both go down; he never rests till blue water is under him again. Yet where is the mariner who will tell thee, “Sir, it was not so much the fear of striking hidden rocks, as the fear of that hideous whiteness that so stirred me?”

annotations.anchor: snow-howdahed Andes
annotations.note: "Howdah" is the canopied seat mounted on an elephant's back; Melville uses it as a verb/adjective, casting the snow-capped Andes peaks as elephants bearing white palanquins. The exotic, imperial register of the word is deliberate — it echoes the chapter's earlier catalogue of white elephants and Eastern monarchs.

annotations.anchor: instead of rainbows speaking hope and solace to his misery, views what seems a boundless churchyard grinning upon him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses
annotations.note: The rainbow as divine covenant of safety derives from Genesis 9:13–16 (God's sign to Noah after the Flood). Melville inverts the biblical promise: the Antarctic sailor receives not God's reassurance but a death-landscape, the covenant replaced by its opposite.

annotations.anchor: lean ice monuments and splintered crosses
annotations.note: Antarctic pack-ice and pressure ridges form irregular vertical spires and jagged shards that early explorers routinely described as resembling gravestones and broken crosses. The image is drawn from actual voyage literature Melville read, including Charles Wilkes's 1845 Narrative of the U.S. Exploring Expedition.

annotations.anchor: boundless churchyard grinning upon him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses
annotations.note: The 'churchyard' image directly anticipates and rhymes with the Lima passage later in the chapter, where the city's whiteness 'spreads over her broken ramparts the rigid pallor of an apoplexy' — both passages yoke whiteness to ruin, death-architecture, and a kind of frozen, grinning horror. The Antarctic churchyard is the natural sublime version of what Lima represents in the human world.

annotations.anchor: instead of rainbows speaking hope and solace to his misery
annotations.note: Beyond the Genesis allusion already noted, the rainbow was a standard emblem of hope in maritime literature and sailor superstition specifically — a fair-weather sign after storm. Melville's inversion is thus doubly pointed: it works against both biblical covenant and the practical seaman's lore that would have been the sailor's own frame of reference, making the betrayal intimate rather than merely theological.

annotations.anchor: the native Indian of Peru
annotations.note: The Peruvian Indian reappears implicitly later in the chapter in the Lima passage ('Old as Pizarro, this whiteness keeps her ruins for ever new'), linking the two moments: the Indian who cannot see the terror of white Andes and the city whose white veil is the very emblem of horror. Melville quietly undermines the earlier claim of Peruvian indifference by showing that Peru is in fact saturated with the whiteness he is describing.

annotations.anchor: shivering and half shipwrecked
annotations.note: The sailor here is already in extremis — 'half shipwrecked' — before the white vision strikes him. This is structurally important to Ishmael's argument: unlike the backwoodsman or the Peruvian Indian, the Antarctic sailor encounters whiteness at the moment of maximum vulnerability, suggesting that the terror of whiteness is not merely intrinsic but is also a function of the perceiver's stripped, undefended condition — a point that feeds directly into the chapter's closing argument about the 'palsied universe' visible only to those who have lost the protective coloring of ordinary association.

annotations.anchor: backwoodsman of the West, who with comparative indifference views an unbounded prairie sheeted with driven snow
annotations.note: This figure is the terrestrial counterpart to the Peruvian Indian and together they form a deliberate pair of 'unimpressed' witnesses bracketing the sailor. Both are defined by habituation to their landscape. The pairing echoes the chapter's structural method throughout — accumulating examples of whiteness that should terrify but do not for the uninitiated, before pivoting to cases where it does. The backwoodsman also recalls the White Steed of the Prairies passage earlier in the chapter, where the same prairie landscape is charged with trembling reverence — the contrast is pointed.

paragraphs.passage: Second: To the native Indian of Peru, the continual sight of the snow-howdahed Andes conveys naught of dread, except, perhaps, in the mere fancying of the eternal frosted desolateness reigning at such vast altitudes, and the natural conceit of what a fearfulness it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Much the same is it with the backwoodsman of the West, who with comparative indifference views an unbounded prairie sheeted with driven snow, no shadow of tree or twig to break the fixed trance of whiteness. Not so the sailor, beholding the scenery of the Antarctic seas; where at times, by some infernal trick of legerdemain in the powers of frost and air, he, shivering and half shipwrecked, instead of rainbows speaking hope and solace to his misery, views what seems a boundless churchyard grinning upon him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.

annotations.anchor: thou surrenderest to a hypo, Ishmael
annotations.note: "Hypo" is short for hypochondria, used in the period to mean depression, morbid anxiety, or low spirits — not the modern sense of imagined illness. Compare the novel's opening: Ishmael goes to sea precisely when a "damp, drizzly November" settles in his soul, his own cure for the hypo.

annotations.anchor: thou surrenderest to a hypo, Ishmael
annotations.note: Direct echo of Chapter 1, where Ishmael describes sailing as his substitute for "pistol and ball" when the hypo overtakes him. The self-interruption here stages the same internal voice that opened the book, now skeptically cross-examining the chapter's entire argument.

annotations.anchor: white-lead chapter about whiteness
annotations.note: The phrase 'white-lead chapter' is the voice's dismissive label for the entire chapter the reader has just been reading — a rare moment of metafictional self-reference in which Melville names and derides his own chapter from within it. The taunt collapses the distance between narrator and reader: we too have just sat through this 'white-lead chapter,' and the accusation of craven philosophizing is implicitly leveled at us as well.

annotations.anchor: thou surrenderest to a hypo, Ishmael
annotations.note: The sudden shift to second person ('thou sayest,' 'thou surrenderest') and the direct address 'Ishmael' is unusual: Ishmael is both the speaker and the one addressed, staging an internal dialogue or self-cross-examination. This is one of the very few moments in the novel where Ishmael's own name is spoken aloud within the narrative, giving the self-accusation a peculiar dramatic force distinct from the novel's opening self-introduction.

annotations.anchor: but a white flag hung out from a craven soul
annotations.note: The white flag image anticipates and ironically inverts the chapter's own closing argument: the chapter ends by describing whiteness as a 'monumental white shroud that wraps all the prospect around him.' The taunt thus uses the chapter's own central symbol against itself — the white flag of surrender is made of the same whiteness whose terror the chapter has been elaborating, tightening the logical trap Ishmael cannot escape.

annotations.anchor: methinks
annotations.note: 'Methinks' carries a Shakespearean register Melville deploys deliberately throughout Moby-Dick. The phrase 'the lady doth protest too much, methinks' (Hamlet III.ii) is a plausible subtext: the taunt accuses Ishmael of protesting — philosophizing — too much, exactly as Gertrude's line accuses excessive performance of an emotion one does not truly feel. The implication is that Ishmael's elaborate argument is itself a symptom of the very anxiety it claims to analyze.

paragraphs.passage: But thou sayest, methinks that white-lead chapter about whiteness is but a white flag hung out from a craven soul; thou surrenderest to a hypo, Ishmael.

annotations.anchor: foaled in some peaceful valley of Vermont, far removed from all beasts of prey
annotations.note: Vermont had no large predators threatening horses by Melville's era; the point is that the colt has zero experiential basis for fear of bison — making the instinctive terror purely innate, not learned.

annotations.anchor: black bisons of distant Oregon
annotations.note: American bison (Bison bison) are dark brown, not black; Melville's "black" is impressionistic, evoking menace. "Oregon" in 1851 still connoted the remote, wild Far West — the Oregon Territory had only become a U.S. territory in 1848.

annotations.anchor: foaled in some peaceful valley of Vermont
annotations.note: The Vermont colt callbacks to the chapter's earlier structural logic: Melville has been building a series of 'untutored' witnesses — the unread Protestant, the untravelled American, the native Indian of Peru — each chosen precisely because their ignorance rules out cultural conditioning as the source of dread. The colt is the reductio ad absurdum of that series, stripping away even human cognition entirely.

annotations.anchor: so that he cannot even see it, but only smells its wild animal muskiness
annotations.note: The deliberate exclusion of sight is philosophically pointed: the entire chapter has been about the terror of whiteness as a visual phenomenon, yet here Melville demonstrates that the deepest instinctive dread bypasses the very sense organ his argument depends on. This momentarily destabilizes his own thesis, suggesting the horror is not in whiteness per se but in something more primordial that whiteness merely makes visible.

annotations.anchor: phrensies of affright
annotations.note: 'Phrensies' is Melville's spelling of 'frenzies,' derived from the Greek 'phrenitis' (inflammation of the brain), carrying a stronger connotation of madness than mere panic. The archaic spelling was already receding in 1851 American usage, and Melville's choice aligns the colt's reaction with the chapter's broader vocabulary of irrational, ungovernable terror — the same register as 'appalled,' 'horror,' and 'panic' used of whiteness throughout.

annotations.anchor: black bisons of distant Oregon
annotations.note: The geographic pairing of Vermont and Oregon spans the continent, mirroring the chapter's earlier geographic sweep (Polar bear / white shark of the tropics; White Mountains of New Hampshire / White Sea; Antarctic seas / Lima). Melville consistently uses continental or global scale to suggest that the terror he is describing is not local or cultural but universal.

paragraphs.passage: Tell me, why this strong young colt, foaled in some peaceful valley of Vermont, far removed from all beasts of prey—why is it that upon the sunniest day, if you but shake a fresh buffalo robe behind him, so that he cannot even see it, but only smells its wild animal muskiness—why will he start, snort, and with bursting eyes paw the ground in phrensies of affright? There is no remembrance in him of any gorings of wild creatures in his green northern home, so that the strange muskiness he smells cannot recall to him anything associated with the experience of former perils; for what knows he, this New England colt, of the black bisons of distant Oregon?

annotations.anchor: the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world
annotations.note: Reading: Melville distinguishes instinct from learned experience to argue that terror of whiteness is ontological, not associative — built into animal nature as a form of pre-cognitive metaphysical knowledge, not a conditioned response.

annotations.anchor: which this instant they may be trampling into dust
annotations.note: Echoes the White Steed of the Prairies passage earlier in this chapter, where vast bison-like herds stream across plains "like an Ohio" — the prairie as a space of overwhelming, annihilating natural force recurs here to clinch the colt analogy.

annotations.anchor: the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world
annotations.note: Melville's formulation anticipates and inverts Lockean empiricism: Locke held that the mind begins as a blank slate, all knowledge derived from sensory experience. The colt's unreasoned terror asserts instead an innate, pre-experiential knowledge of evil — a position closer to Calvinist doctrine of innate depravity, which Melville would have encountered through his New England Protestant background and which haunts the chapter's closing theological anxieties.

annotations.anchor: the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world
annotations.note: Directly anticipates the chapter's closing philosophical turn — 'though in many of its aspects this visible world seems formed in love, the invisible spheres were formed in fright' — making the colt episode not merely an analogy but the structural hinge between the catalogue of examples and the chapter's metaphysical conclusion. The 'demonism' here is the same force that the final paragraphs locate in the colorless void behind all visible nature.

annotations.anchor: the rending, goring bison herds are as present as to the deserted wild foal of the prairies
annotations.note: The phrase 'deserted wild foal of the prairies' echoes the chapter's earlier description of the White Steed as 'elected Xerxes of vast herds' — the foal is the inverse image of that sovereign horse, abandoned and vulnerable rather than commanding, suggesting Melville is consciously dismantling the sublime prairie horse-image he constructed earlier to expose the terror beneath it.

annotations.anchor: Though thousands of miles from Oregon, still when he smells that savage musk
annotations.note: 'Oregon' here functions as a synecdoche for the far western wilderness, but Melville's choice is precise: Oregon Territory in the early 1850s was the outermost edge of American expansion, legally organized only in 1848, and still associated in Eastern readers' minds with trackless, ungovernable wildness. The geographical distance — Vermont to Oregon — is the maximum imaginable within the American frame, reinforcing that the colt's knowledge transcends any possible experiential transmission.

paragraphs.passage: No: but here thou beholdest even in a dumb brute, the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, still when he smells that savage musk, the rending, goring bison herds are as present as to the deserted wild foal of the prairies, which this instant they may be trampling into dust.

annotations.anchor: muffled rollings of a milky sea
annotations.note: Picks up the chapter's earlier image of a mariner sailing through "a midnight sea of milky whiteness" — the three-part list here is the explicit payoff of those preceding examples, now gathered and named as analogues to the colt's instinctive terror.

annotations.anchor: festooned frosts of mountains
annotations.note: "Festooned" (garlands hung in loops) applied to frost is deliberately decorative — the word's festive, ornamental connotation clashes with "bleak," enacting the chapter's central argument that whiteness wears beauty as a disguise for horror.

annotations.anchor: windrowed snows of prairies
annotations.note: "Windrowed": a windrow is a long ridge of cut hay or grain raked into a line for drying. Applied to snow, it means drifts combed into parallel ridges by wind — a precise agricultural term displaced into a desolate landscape.

annotations.anchor: muffled rollings of a milky sea
annotations.note: "Muffled" does double duty: acoustically, it suppresses the sound that would normally alert a mariner to danger (cf. the chapter's earlier contrast between the audible roar of breakers, which merely sharpens faculties, and the silent milky sea, which produces superstitious dread) — the very quality of muteness that Melville identifies a few sentences later as one of the two conditions that make whiteness most terrible to the imagination.

annotations.anchor: festooned frosts of mountains
annotations.note: Picks up the chapter's earlier mention of "the White Mountains of New Hampshire" and the "gigantic ghostliness" their bare name produces — the mountains example, previously offered as a psychological puzzle, is here re-enlisted as one of the three analogues to the colt's instinct, completing its argumentative function.

annotations.anchor: all these, to Ishmael
annotations.note: The sudden first-person naming — 'to Ishmael' rather than 'to me' — is the only moment in the chapter where Ishmael refers to himself in the third person. The distancing effect mirrors the chapter's opening claim that his horror of whiteness is 'vague, nameless,' almost impossible to own in the first person; naming himself as a character rather than a narrator enacts that self-alienation.

annotations.anchor: windrowed snows of prairies
annotations.note: Completes a trio that maps onto the chapter's own geographic sequence: sea (the milky-sea mariner passage), mountains (the White Mountains / Antarctic-seas passage), and prairies (the backwoodsman-viewing-snow passage) — the three-item list is thus a compressed recapitulation of the chapter's own illustrative geography, not merely a rhetorical flourish.

paragraphs.passage: Thus, then, the muffled rollings of a milky sea; the bleak rustlings of the festooned frosts of mountains; the desolate shiftings of the windrowed snows of prairies; all these, to Ishmael, are as the shaking of that buffalo robe to the frightened colt!

annotations.anchor: the mystic sign gives forth such hints
annotations.note: "Sign" here carries its older semiotic weight — a thing that stands for something beyond itself — rather than mere signal or symptom. The phrase frames whiteness as a symbol whose referent cannot be named, only gestured at.

annotations.anchor: the invisible spheres were formed in fright
annotations.note: Echoes Neoplatonic and Gnostic cosmologies in which the material world was created by a lesser, fearful demiurge rather than a benevolent God — a tradition running from Plotinus through the Gnostics that Melville would have encountered in his wide theological reading.

annotations.anchor: somewhere those things must exist
annotations.note: The logical structure here is crucial and easily missed: Ishmael does not claim to know what the nameless things are, only that the instinctive response to the sign guarantees their existence — an argument from affect to ontology. This mirrors Kant's argument from moral feeling to the postulation of noumena, and anticipates the chapter's closing move where the 'invisible spheres' are asserted as real precisely because the visible world's lovingness is exposed as illusion.

annotations.anchor: Though neither knows where lie the nameless things
annotations.note: Picks up the chapter's own opening confession — 'so mystical and well nigh ineffable was it, that I almost despair of putting it in a comprehensible form' — completing a frame: the chapter begins by admitting the horror cannot be named and ends by insisting the unnamed thing nonetheless exists. The structural echo reinforces that the chapter's argument is not an explanation but a demonstration of inexplicability.

annotations.anchor: the invisible spheres were formed in fright
annotations.note: 'Spheres' retains its Ptolemaic-Platonic resonance of the celestial orbs — the concentric heavenly shells of traditional cosmology — giving the sentence a precise cosmogonic claim: not merely that fear underlies human psychology, but that the architecture of the universe itself was constituted by it. This sharpens the contrast with 'this visible world,' which occupies only the sublunary realm in that same cosmological scheme.

annotations.anchor: Though in many of its aspects this visible world seems formed in love
annotations.note: The phrasing closely echoes Schiller's 'Ode to Joy' ('Freude, schöner Götterfunken') and its Romantic-idealist tradition of reading benevolence into natural order, a tradition Melville systematically dismantles throughout the chapter. The word 'seems' is doing the critical work: the lovingness is phenomenal appearance, not noumenal fact.

annotations.anchor: as with the colt
annotations.note: The colt analogy was introduced several sentences earlier as an illustration of instinctive, non-associative dread — dread with no personal experiential basis. Returning to it here with 'as with the colt' closes that analogy by equating Ishmael's response to whiteness with the colt's response to the buffalo musk: both are signs of something real and dangerous that neither perceiver has directly encountered, making Ishmael's terror epistemically respectable rather than merely hysterical. This directly answers the taunt — 'thou surrenderest to a hypo, Ishmael' — issued earlier in the chapter.

paragraphs.passage: Though neither knows where lie the nameless things of which the mystic sign gives forth such hints; yet with me, as with the colt, somewhere those things must exist. Though in many of its aspects this visible world seems formed in love, the invisible spheres were formed in fright.

annotations.anchor: incantation of this whiteness
annotations.note: "Incantation" (from Latin incantare, to sing a spell into) frames whiteness as an active enchantment rather than a passive quality — the chapter has been attempting to break the spell by naming it, and here Melville concedes the attempt has failed.

annotations.anchor: the very veil of the Christian’s Deity
annotations.note: Draws on Exodus 33–34, where Moses cannot see God's face directly, and on the Temple veil (Matthew 27:51) torn at the Crucifixion. The veil simultaneously conceals and signals divine presence — whiteness functions the same way: it marks the sacred while hiding what lies behind it.

annotations.anchor: intensifying agent in things the most appalling to mankind
annotations.note: Recaps the chapter's counter-catalogue: the white bear, white shark, the Albino, the White Squall, Lima's white veil, and the milky Antarctic sea — all cases where whiteness amplifies rather than sanctifies terror.

annotations.anchor: incantation of this whiteness
annotations.note: The word 'incantation' echoes the chapter's earlier admission that whiteness exerts a 'sorcery' over us ('found to exert over us the same sorcery, however modified'), binding the closing movement to the methodological pivot where Melville proposed to find a 'chance clue' to the hidden cause — a clue he now confesses has not been found.

annotations.anchor: the very veil of the Christian’s Deity
annotations.note: Alludes to Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians (3:12–18), where the veil over Moses's face becomes a figure for the veil over the minds of those who cannot perceive divine truth — a veil 'done away in Christ.' Melville inverts the Pauline promise: the veil is not lifted but identified with whiteness itself, which remains permanently opaque.

annotations.anchor: most meaning symbol of spiritual things
annotations.note: 'Most meaning' is a compressed superlative — not 'most meaningful' but 'most laden with meaning,' preserving meaning as an active, almost aggressive property. The phrasing anticipates the closing paradox: the thing most saturated with significance is also the thing that, stripped of context, signifies nothing — 'a dumb blankness, full of meaning.'

annotations.anchor: intensifying agent in things the most appalling to mankind
annotations.note: The chemical/alchemical register of 'intensifying agent' is precise and deliberate: whiteness does not create terror but amplifies a terror already present in the object, exactly as a photographic intensifier deepens an existing image. This frames whiteness as a medium or catalyst rather than a cause, which is why the chapter cannot locate a cause — it has been looking for the wrong kind of thing.

annotations.anchor: appeals with such power to the soul
annotations.note: Directly recalls the chapter's opening confession — 'It was the whiteness of the whale that above all things appalled me' and 'I almost despair of putting it in a comprehensible form' — closing a bracket around the entire chapter and confirming that the narrator's personal terror, deferred to the opening, has still not been explained even after the full philosophical excursion.

paragraphs.passage: But not yet have we solved the incantation of this whiteness, and learned why it appeals with such power to the soul; and more strange and far more portentous—why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaning symbol of spiritual things, nay, the very veil of the Christian’s Deity; and yet should be as it is, the intensifying agent in things the most appalling to mankind.

annotations.anchor: heartless voids and immensities of the universe
annotations.note: Reading: Melville anticipates the existential vertigo of post-Newtonian cosmology — Pascal's 'eternal silence of infinite spaces' — framing whiteness as the color of a universe indifferent to human meaning, not merely aesthetically blank.

annotations.anchor: colourless, all-colour of atheism
annotations.note: Reading: the phrase equates optical totality with theological nullity — if white contains all colors yet signifies nothing, it becomes the emblem of a universe that means everything and nothing simultaneously, the aesthetic form of godlessness.

annotations.anchor: other theory of the natural philosophers
annotations.note: Refers to Locke's distinction between primary and secondary qualities: color is a secondary quality existing only in the perceiver's mind, not in objects themselves. Melville would have encountered this via popular scientific writing; it was standard educated currency by 1851.

annotations.anchor: all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within
annotations.note: Echoes Matthew 23:27 — Christ's denunciation of hypocrites as 'whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones.' Melville extends the biblical image from moral hypocrisy to cosmic deception.

annotations.anchor: wilful travellers in Lapland, who refuse to wear coloured and colouring glasses upon their eyes
annotations.note: Snow blindness in Arctic regions was a documented hazard; tinted goggles or slitted bone visors were used by indigenous peoples and explorers. The 'wilful' traveller who refuses them courts blindness — here, the blindness of seeing reality without the mediating illusions of color.

annotations.anchor: the palsied universe lies before us a leper
annotations.note: 'Palsied' means paralyzed, not merely trembling — from medieval Latin paralysis via 'palsy.' The coupling with 'leper' sustains a single image: a universe both motionless and diseased, its white surface the symptom of inner corruption rather than purity.

annotations.anchor: stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation
annotations.note: The spatial metaphor — annihilation attacking from behind, unseen — recapitulates the chapter's earlier logic that whiteness terrifies precisely because it is mute and gives no warning, unlike the tiger in his 'heraldic coat.' The horror is not confrontational but ambush; the universe offers no legible threat to brace against.

annotations.anchor: colourless, all-colour of atheism
annotations.note: The oxymoron echoes Carlyle's 'Natural Supernaturalism' in Sartor Resartus (1833–34), where the stripping away of symbolic 'clothes' from the universe reveals a blank, godless substrate. Melville was a close reader of Carlyle; the 'all-colour' that signifies nothing parallels Carlyle's universe denuded of its wonder-garments.

annotations.anchor: other theory of the natural philosophers
annotations.note: Beyond Locke, the immediate scientific referent is Newton's Opticks (1704), Book I, which demonstrated that white light is not a simple entity but a compound of all spectral colors separable by a prism. Melville's phrasing 'other theory' distinguishes this optical account from the preceding cosmological one, and Newton is the more precise source than Locke for the color-as-secondary-quality argument as applied to light itself.

annotations.anchor: all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot
annotations.note: The harlot image also draws on Proverbs 7, where the 'strange woman' with her 'fair speech' and 'flattering lips' leads men to destruction — her allure concealing death. Melville's 'deified Nature' as harlot thus conflates the Matthean whited sepulchre with the Proverbial femme fatale, compounding the sense of beautiful surfaces masking lethal interiors.

annotations.anchor: the mystical cosmetic which produces every one of her hues
annotations.note: 'Cosmetic' retains its Greek root: kosmetikos, from kosmein, to arrange or adorn — related to kosmos, the ordered universe. Melville's choice is precise and ironic: the very word for superficial beautification shares its root with the word for the ordered cosmos, implying that cosmic order is itself merely decorative, a painted surface over void.

annotations.anchor: Wonder ye then at the fiery hunt
annotations.note: The closing rhetorical question mirrors the chapter's opening move, which promised that without this explanation 'all these chapters might be naught.' The 'fiery hunt' also picks up the fire imagery latent throughout the novel's Ahab chapters — notably the corposants scene foreshadowed — and sets whiteness (cold, blank) against fire (passionate, purposive) as the novel's governing antithesis.

annotations.anchor: dumb blankness, full of meaning
annotations.note: The paradox — blankness that is simultaneously full of meaning — is the chapter's central epistemological knot, and it callbacks directly to the opening admission that the horror was 'so mystical and well nigh ineffable' that Ishmael 'almost despair[ed] of putting it in a comprehensible form.' The chapter ends by confirming that the horror resists articulation not because it is empty but because it is over-full: meaning without referent.

paragraphs.passage: Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation, when beholding the white depths of the milky way? Or is it, that as in essence whiteness is not so much a colour as the visible absence of colour; and at the same time the concrete of all colours; is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows—a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink? And when we consider that other theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly hues—every stately or lovely emblazoning—the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods; yea, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls; all these are but subtile deceits, not actually inherent in substances, but only laid on from without; so that all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within; and when we proceed further, and consider that the mystical cosmetic which produces every one of her hues, the great principle of light, for ever remains white or colorless in itself, and if operating without medium upon matter, would touch all objects, even tulips and roses, with its own blank tinge—pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper; and like wilful travellers in Lapland, who refuse to wear coloured and colouring glasses upon their eyes, so the wretched infidel gazes himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps all the prospect around him. And of all these things the Albino whale was the symbol. Wonder ye then at the fiery hunt?
